I01.q: A jeweller in Jaipur asks you for a 60-second reel. Before you plan any shots, what should you ask him first?
options: Who should watch it, and what should they do after?
Which camera and lens would he like me to use?
Gear choices come later and depend on what the reel needs to achieve.
Which trending song would he like in the reel?
Music is a style choice, and you cannot pick it well until you know the goal.
I01.why: Knowing the viewer and the result you want lets you judge every later choice, from shots to music to length.

I01.q: You are making a promo for a wedding planner. The aim is to get engaged couples to book a call. You have time for one more setup. Which do you film?
options: A past couple saying how calm the planner kept their big day
A slow drone shot of the venue, since it looks very grand
It looks impressive, but it shows the venue, not why a couple should call this planner.
A close detail shot of the flowers and the table decor
Pretty decor does not tell a couple what working with this planner feels like.
I01.why: A real couple speaking about the experience talks straight to the viewers you want and gives them a reason to call.

I01.q: You are making a short film about a potter in Khurja. Which plan gives you a story, not just a subject?
options: Follow one big order she fears she cannot finish in time
Film her wheel, her kiln and her shelves in good light
These are lovely shots of her world, but nothing in them changes.
Interview her about the long history of pottery in town
History gives background, but it does not put anything at stake for her now.
I01.why: A deadline she might miss creates tension and change, which is what turns a person into a story.

I01.q: In "Visual Storytelling in Filmmaking", what is the main approach the video encourages?
options: Let the pictures carry meaning, so viewers work it out themselves
Add more voiceover so the audience never misses the point
Explaining everything in words is the opposite of telling the story with images.
Use the most beautiful shots, even if they add no meaning
The video is about images that tell the story, not images that only look good.
I01.why: The video shows how a planned, image-led approach lets shots do the telling, which keeps viewers engaged.

I01.q: Your film shows a school annual day through the eyes of a nervous child waiting to perform. The principal starts a speech. How do you film it?
options: From the side of the stage, near the child waiting to go on
From the front row, as a clean, steady shot of the principal
A clean front view is nice, but it leaves the child and shows the event like any guest would.
Cut evenly between the child, the parents and the teachers
Sharing time equally spreads the view across many people and weakens the child's experience.
I01.why: Filming from where the child is keeps us inside their nerves, even during a moment about someone else.

I01.q: In the DSLRguide video on composition and framing, what is the key idea about where you place a person in the frame?
options: Where they sit in the frame changes how we feel about them
It is mostly about keeping the frame balanced and tidy
Balance can matter, but the video stresses that framing carries ideas and emotion.
It should follow the same fixed rules in every scene
The video shows framing changing with what the scene needs to say, not fixed rules.
I01.why: Composition, meaning how the frame is arranged, tells the viewer how to read a person. For example, someone small in a big empty frame can feel alone.

I01.q: Your 45-second promo for a tailor's shop is 5 seconds too long. One clip is a slow-motion shot of cloth blowing in a fan. What do you do?
options: Remove the cloth shot and keep the tailor measuring a customer
Keep the cloth shot and speed up the other clips a little
Speeding up useful clips to save a pretty but empty shot makes the whole video weaker.
Move the cloth shot to the opening, since starts should look nice
An opening shot should pull viewers in with meaning, not just look attractive.
I01.why: The measuring shot tells viewers what the tailor does and how he works, while the cloth shot adds nothing they did not know.

I01.q: You are filming a paratha seller in Old Delhi. You already have a wide shot of his stall. What is the best next shot?
options: A close-up of his hands flipping parathas at speed
A second wide shot of the stall from across the lane
Another wide repeats what the viewer has already seen.
A sunset timelapse over the rooftops nearby
It looks lovely, but it tells us nothing about him or his work.
I01.why: The close-up shows his skill and speed, which the wide shot could not, so the viewer learns something.

I01.q: You are editing a documentary about a girl training for a state kabaddi trial. You have scenes of money worries at home and a knee injury two weeks before the trial. Where does the injury go?
options: Late, after the money worries, close to trial day
Right at the start, to hook viewers in the first seconds
Using your biggest problem first leaves nothing bigger to come, so the middle feels flat.
Leave it out, since it makes the film feel too sad
The injury is the hardest test she faces, and cutting it removes the strongest pressure.
I01.why: Putting the worst setback near the end, after smaller problems, makes the pressure grow and the trial matter more.

I01.q: An NGO's video has three family stories. The toughest story comes first and the mildest comes last. Test viewers lose interest halfway. What is the best fix?
options: Open with the mildest story and end with the toughest one
Add livelier music under the middle part of the video
Music can lift energy for a moment, but it cannot fix a structure that runs downhill.
Trim all three stories so they are exactly the same length
Equal length does not change the order, so the video still gets weaker as it goes.
I01.why: When each part feels more serious than the one before, viewers sense rising pressure and keep watching.

I01.q: The family wants a tender, emotional video for a grandmother's 80th birthday. Your rough cut uses a fast party song and quick dance clips. What do you change?
options: Use slower clips with room to breathe and a gentle track
Keep the fast song and add a warm colour filter on top
A warm filter helps a little, but fast music and cuts still push the mood toward party energy.
Add even more quick cuts so the day feels full of life
More quick cuts make it more energetic, which moves further away from tender.
I01.why: Holding moments longer and using softer music gives viewers time to feel, which creates a tender mood.

I01.q: In "How Editors Cut the Same Scene in 2 Completely Different Ways", what makes the two documentary cuts feel so different?
options: The order of moments, the music and the pauses between them
Each version was made from different footage of the scene
The point of the video is that the same footage can be read two ways.
Only the colour grading was changed between the two cuts
The video shows structure, music and spacing doing the work, not colour alone.
I01.why: The editors show that arranging the same material differently, with different music and spacing, changes how viewers understand it.
I01.video: How Editors Cut the Same Scene in 2 Completely Different Ways

I02.q: A dance academy owner in Pune says, "Make a nice video for our Instagram." Which line would you write as the goal in your brief?
options: Get parents of kids aged 6 to 12 in Pune to book a free trial class.
Show the studio looking modern and bright with slow-motion dance shots.
This describes how the video looks, not who it is for or what they should do.
Make a reel so good that everyone in the city shares it.
"Everyone" is not a real viewer, and shares alone do not tell you if the video worked.
I02.why: It names a specific group of people and one action you can count later. That makes it easy to plan shots and check results.

I02.q: In the Ziflow video, which set of things does a creative brief pin down at the start?
options: The aim, the target audience, what gets handed over, and the limits of the work.
The camera, lenses, lighting kit and crew list for the shoot day.
These are production details that come later, once the brief is agreed.
The final script, the music track and the full edit timeline.
These are made after the brief, not written into it.
I02.why: The video covers objectives, audience, deliverables and scope. Agreeing on these early keeps the whole team working toward the same result.
I02.video: What Is a Creative Brief? How to Write One That Aligns Your Team

I02.q: A jeweller in Jaipur wants a launch video. You have a 20-minute first meeting. Which question is most likely to save you a reshoot later?
options: Who besides you has to approve the final cut?
Would you like some drone shots of the shop?
This is about technique and can be decided later, once the goal is clear.
What song would you like playing in the background?
Music can be picked later and rarely forces a reshoot.
I02.why: If a partner or family elder sees the video only at the end, they may ask for big changes. Knowing who signs off lets you include them early.

I02.q: A boutique owner says, "We need the video soon." What is the best thing to do next?
options: Ask for an exact date and what event or post it is meant for.
Promise about a week and adjust later if needed.
A guess can clash with their real date and cause stress for both of you.
Say yes and fit it in when your schedule frees up.
Without a fixed date you may deliver after the moment they needed it.
I02.why: "Soon" means different things to different people. A real date, tied to a reason, lets you plan the shoot and edit properly.

I02.q: A Kolkata sweet shop wants a 60-second video to sell Diwali gift boxes to offices. They also want their history since 1952, all 40 sweets, catering and a new branch. What do you do?
options: Build it around the Diwali boxes and save the other topics for later videos.
Show all 40 sweets quickly so no product is missed.
A fast list of sweets buries the gift box message the client actually needs.
Give each topic about ten seconds so everything fits.
Splitting time five ways means no topic is strong enough to make people act.
I02.why: Office buyers need one clear reason to order. The other topics can become their own short videos.

I02.q: You are editing a 30-second reel for a home tutor app. You have a lovely drone shot of the city that has nothing to do with the app. What do you do?
options: Cut it, because it does not help viewers understand the app.
Keep it as the opening because it looks expensive.
A pretty shot that is off topic wastes the first seconds, when viewers decide to stay.
Trim the other shots to make room for it.
This weakens the useful shots to fit in one that adds nothing to the message.
I02.why: In a short video every second must earn its place. A shot you love is still wrong if it does not serve the message.

I02.q: You send a Bengaluru café owner five sample clips for her video. She replies, "I like all of them!" What do you do next?
options: Ask what she likes in each one, like the light, pace or colour, and note it.
Take that as approval and mix ideas from all five clips.
Five different styles mixed together can look messy and may not be what she pictured.
Pick your own favourite of the five and start planning.
You are still guessing what she wants, so you may disagree after the shoot.
I02.why: Liking a clip is not the same as agreeing on a look. Pinning down the exact things she likes gives you a clear target before filming.

I02.q: In Robin Piree's video, what is the main job of a director's treatment?
options: To explain your creative approach in words and pictures so the client can imagine the film.
To list the budget, crew rates and payment schedule for the project.
Money details go in a quote or contract, not in the treatment.
To give a shot-by-shot technical plan for the camera team.
That is a shot list, which comes after the creative idea is agreed.
I02.why: The treatment sells and explains the idea. It helps the client feel the mood and story before anything is filmed.
I02.video: How To Write A Director's Treatment (FAST)?

I02.q: A coaching centre agreed to "a promo video." After the edit, they ask for vertical reels, Hindi subtitles and five rounds of changes, all free. What should you have done at the start?
options: Listed each version, its length and shape, and how many change rounds are included.
Charged a higher price up front to cover any extra requests.
A higher price without a clear list still leaves both sides arguing about what is included.
Shared all the raw footage so they could make their own reels.
This hands over your work without fixing the real problem of an unclear agreement.
I02.why: A clear list of versions, sizes and revisions shows both sides what is included. Extra requests can then be quoted as extra work.

I02.q: In Caleb Pike's corporate video guide, why does he gather a brief before shooting for a business client?
options: So you and the client agree on aims and outputs before time and money are spent.
So the client cannot ask for any changes once filming starts.
A brief sets direction, but changes still happen and need to be planned for.
So you can choose the gear and crew size before anything else.
Gear choices follow from the brief's aims; they are not the reason for it.
I02.why: Business clients often have several people with opinions. A shared brief keeps everyone on the same plan and protects you from surprises later.

I03.q: You will film an interview in a small tailoring shop. On your visit you find only one socket, behind the counter, and the sewing machine uses it. What do you do?
options: Ask the owner which socket you may use, and pack extension cords and spare charged batteries.
Note it down and plan to sort out charging when you arrive on the shoot day.
Leaving it for the day means you may run out of battery in the middle of the shoot.
Plan to unplug the sewing machine whenever you need to charge a battery.
This disturbs the owner's work, and nobody has agreed to it.
I03.why: Asking first and packing cords and batteries means power can't stop your shoot. You solve the problem days before it can hurt you.

I03.q: A client wants a 6 pm interview at a street-side café. You visited the café at 11 am and it was calm. What is the biggest risk you have missed?
options: Evening traffic noise, and a low sun that may hit the camera or the speaker's face.
The café staff may be busier and slower to serve tea to your crew.
Slow tea is a small comfort issue; it does not spoil your picture or sound.
Your camera may behave differently in the evening than in the morning.
The camera works the same way; the place around it is what changes.
I03.why: Light and noise change a lot over a day. A morning visit tells you little about 6 pm traffic or where the sun will sit.

I03.q: In the StudioBinder video, how is a technical scout different from simply finding a place that looks good?
options: It checks whether the crew and gear can actually work there on the shoot day.
It is mainly about choosing the best angles for the poster and thumbnail.
Picking good-looking angles is part of the first scout, not the technical one.
It is mainly a chance to bargain a lower rent with the location owner.
Money talks may happen, but the tech scout is about practical working conditions.
I03.why: A place can look perfect and still fail on noise, power or getting gear in. The tech scout tests those practical needs before production.
I03.video: Location Scouting Explained — with Tech Scout Checklist

I03.q: You have 90 minutes to film a bakery owner for her promo video. She warns you she may have to leave early to meet a supplier. What do you film first?
options: Her main interview answers, then the shots of the bakery if time allows.
Slow slider shots of the cakes to set the mood before she sits down.
These look nice, but the video still works without them; her answers can't be replaced.
A wide shot outside the shop so the video can open on the street.
You can get the outside shot any time, even after she leaves.
I03.why: Her words are the heart of the video and only she can give them. Film what you can't replace first, and add the extras later.

I03.q: According to "A Director's Guide to Shot Listing", what is the main job of a shot list?
options: To turn the director's coverage plan into a document the crew can follow on set.
To list every possible angle so you never have to make choices on set.
A shot list is a set of choices, not every angle anyone could think of.
To replace the script once filming starts so the crew needs only one page.
The shot list works alongside the script; it does not replace it.
I03.why: The director decides how each scene will be covered. The shot list writes that plan down so camera and crew work from the same page.
I03.video: A Director's Guide to Shot Listing

I03.q: Late at night, the temple you planned to film at in Pune says you must move to a hall next door. Your crew of four meets at 7 am. What do you do?
options: Send an updated sheet with the new address to all four and confirm each one has seen it.
Tell the director tonight and let the news spread to the others.
Passing it along by word of mouth often misses someone or gets the details wrong.
Keep the old plan and explain the change to everyone when they arrive.
People will go to the wrong place first and lose time in the morning.
I03.why: One clear written update reaches everyone with the same details. Checking that each person read it stops anyone going to the old address.

I03.q: In "A Producer's Guide to Call Sheets", which set of details belongs on a call sheet?
options: Contacts, address, weather and the nearest hospital, along with call times.
The full script and the lens chosen for every shot in the scene.
Those belong in the script and shot list, not the call sheet.
Each person's fee for the day and the overall project budget.
Money details are private and do not help people get to set.
I03.why: A call sheet gives practical day information: who to call, where to go, what to expect and how to stay safe. Creative and money details live elsewhere.
I03.video: A Producer's Guide to Call Sheets

I03.q: At a family wedding shoot, the bride's uncle keeps telling your camera operator where to stand. The operator is getting confused. What do you do?
options: Politely ask the uncle to share his ideas with the director, who talks to the family.
Tell the operator to follow the uncle, since he is part of the family.
Now the camera person has two bosses, and the director's plan falls apart.
Ignore the uncle completely and hope he gets tired and walks away.
This can upset the family; someone still needs to listen to him.
I03.why: One person should speak with the family and give camera its directions. That keeps the operator focused and the family feeling heard.

I03.q: Your crew of three is filming an interview. A loud bike horn spoils one answer, but the speaker keeps talking. What should happen?
options: The sound person tells the director, who asks for that answer once more.
The camera person stops recording at once without telling anyone.
Camera should not decide on takes alone; it confuses the speaker and the director.
Nobody says anything, and you try to clean the horn out in the edit.
A horn over speech is very hard to remove later; it is easier to record again.
I03.why: Sound hears the problem, and the director decides on the take. Each person doing their own part fixes it quickly and calmly.

I03.q: You have ₹20,000 left for a series of interviews with shop owners in busy markets. What do you buy first?
options: A lavalier kit, a small clip-on mic worn on the shirt, plus a recorder.
A gimbal, a handheld stabiliser, for smooth walking shots in the market.
Smooth shots are nice, but shaky footage is easier to live with than unclear voices.
A second fast lens for a softer background behind each shop owner.
A soft background is a bonus; the interviews fail if people can't be heard.
I03.why: In a noisy market, clear voices are the hardest thing to rescue later. A clip-on mic close to the mouth solves that at the source.

I03.q: In Curren Sheldon's budget tutorial, what does he set out before filling in any costs?
options: Written assumptions, like the number of shoot days, crew size and locations.
The price of the most expensive camera he hopes to use on the film.
Starting with gear prices skips the basic facts that drive every other cost.
The client's total amount, split evenly across every category.
Splitting money evenly ignores what the film actually needs.
I03.why: Costs come from facts like days, people and places. Writing those down first makes every number easy to check and change.
I03.video: How To Make A Film Budget | Tutorial + Free Download

I03.q: In the same tutorial, what does "below the line" mean in a film budget?
options: Crew, equipment, locations and other day-to-day production costs.
The writer, director and lead actors who shape the film creatively.
Those key creative people are above the line, not below it.
Extra costs you can cut first if the money starts running low.
Below the line is a category of costs, not a list of optional extras.
I03.why: Budgets split key creative people (above the line) from the crew and practical costs of making the film (below the line).
I03.video: How To Make A Film Budget | Tutorial + Free Download

I03.q: You are filming a company's annual event with one camera. A week before, what is the smartest step to protect the shoot?
options: Arrange a second body or phone, test it, and agree when it will take over.
Get your main camera serviced and trust that it will not fail.
Servicing helps, but any camera can still fail and you would have nothing.
Tell the client that if the camera fails, the event can't be filmed.
This passes the risk to the client instead of solving it.
I03.why: A tested spare that everyone knows about means a failure costs you minutes, not the whole event. Deciding it early keeps you calm on the day.

I03.q: Your documentary depends on one weaver in Varanasi, and he says he might be travelling that week. What do you do?
options: Line up a second weaver now and tell the client which one you will film if needed.
Wait until the shoot day and find someone at the market if he is away.
Searching on the day wastes crew time and you may find nobody suitable.
Move the whole shoot to a later month without checking his dates.
This delays everything for a problem that may never happen.
I03.why: Having another person ready keeps the shoot on track either way. Telling the client early means nobody is surprised.

I03.q: In the AI breakdown walkthrough, what do you do with the schedule changes it suggests?
options: Check each one against the crew, location and production limits before accepting it.
Accept them all to save time.
The tool doesn’t know every real-world limit.
Ignore them all.
Some suggestions can save real time. Check them.
I03.why: AI suggestions are proposals. You approve them.

I03.q: An AI tool moves your night market scene to the morning to save a day. What’s the problem?
options: The market only looks right at night, so the scene changes.
There’s no problem. A day saved is good.
Saving a day isn’t worth losing the scene.
Mornings are harder to light.
The bigger issue is that the scene no longer matches the script.
I03.why: Check that changes keep what the story needs.

I04.q: At a sangeet, you set your camera to 50 frames per second so you can slow down the dancing later. Which shutter speed should you pick?
options: 1/100 of a second
1/50 of a second
That suits 25 frames a second. At 50 frames it gives more blur than looks natural.
1/1000 of a second
Such a fast shutter freezes each frame, so the movement looks jerky.
I04.why: At 50 frames a second, a shutter of 1/100 gives each frame the right amount of motion blur, so the dancing looks smooth.

I04.q: You want smooth slow motion of a kite flying. Based on the video, what should you do?
options: Record at a high frame rate, then play it at the normal rate
Record at 24 or 25 frames, then slow it down in the edit
There are too few frames to stretch, so the slowed clip looks jerky.
Keep the normal frame rate and use a faster shutter
A faster shutter changes blur, not speed, so it cannot create slow motion.
I04.why: Recording more frames each second and playing them at the normal rate spreads the action over more time, which gives smooth slow motion.
I04.video: What is Frame Rate? Frames Per Second Explained

I04.q: You film a puja in a home lit by warm yellow bulbs. On auto, the colour shifts every time someone in a bright saree walks past. What do you do?
options: Choose a fixed setting of about 3200K and keep it for every shot
Leave it on auto and fix each clip in the edit later
Clips that change colour in the middle of a shot are slow to fix and rarely match well.
Switch to the daylight preset for cleaner, brighter colours
A daylight setting under yellow bulbs makes everything look very orange.
I04.why: K stands for Kelvin, a number for the colour of light. A fixed value that suits the bulbs stops the camera from guessing again on every shot.

I04.q: Your camera is set to about 5600K, but you are filming under ordinary tungsten bulbs. Based on the video, how will the footage look?
options: Too orange or yellow
Too blue or cold
Blue comes from a low Kelvin setting in daylight, which is the opposite case.
Natural and correct
5600K matches daylight, not tungsten bulbs, so the colour will be off.
I04.why: Tungsten light is much warmer, around 3200K, so a daylight setting leaves its warm colour uncorrected and the image looks orange.
I04.video: Color Temperature Explained: White Balance Fundamentals

I04.q: You are interviewing a shop owner standing in front of a bright street doorway at noon. The face looks dark on your screen. What is the best move?
options: Turn them so the doorway is not behind, or add light to the face
Expose for the bright street so it keeps all its detail
The face will stay dark, and the face is what the viewer needs to see.
Raise exposure until the face is bright and ignore the doorway
The street will turn pure white with no detail, which looks careless.
I04.why: Reducing the gap in brightness between the face and the background lets you show the face well without losing the bright area behind.

I04.q: The video stresses watching the highlights, the brightest parts of the image. Why do cinematographers take such care with them?
options: Once they turn pure white, the detail cannot be brought back
Bright areas always add a lot of grain to the picture
Grain mostly shows up in dark areas and at high ISO, not in highlights.
Highlights decide the white balance of the whole shot
White balance is set separately and does not depend on how bright the highlights are.
I04.why: Clipped highlights hold no information, so no edit can recover them. That is why tools like zebras (striped warning lines on the screen) are used to check them while shooting.

I04.q: A client runs a home bakery from a small kitchen. They want one shot that shows the whole workspace, but you cannot step back. What do you use?
options: A lens around 16mm to 24mm from the doorway
A lens around 85mm pushed into a corner
An 85mm lens shows only a narrow slice, so you would see one counter at best.
A 50mm lens and several pans across the room
Panning shows the room in parts, not in one clear shot as the client wants.
I04.why: A short focal length takes in a broad view, so you can show a whole small room even with your back to the wall.

I04.q: At a wedding, you want a temple behind the couple to look big and close to them in the frame. What do you do?
options: Move far back and use a 100mm or longer lens
Stand close to the couple with a 24mm lens
A wide lens up close makes the background look smaller and further away.
Stay where you are and crop in during the edit
Cropping loses quality and does not change how near the background feels.
I04.why: A long lens used from a distance squeezes the space, so the background looks larger and closer to the subject.

I04.q: You film a jewellery piece on a table with the camera on a tripod. A hand reaches in to pick it up, and the focus jumps to the hand. What should you do?
options: Switch to manual, focus on the jewellery, and shoot again
Turn on tracking autofocus and select the jewellery
Tracking can still jump to the hand when it comes closer or covers the piece.
Open the aperture wider so the hand goes soft
A wider aperture makes the sharp area thinner, so any jump becomes more obvious.
I04.why: Manual focus stays on the product no matter what enters the frame, which a fixed product shot needs.

I04.q: A man talks at a table and his phone starts ringing behind him. You want viewers to look from him to the phone. What technique does the video show for this?
options: Shift the sharp area from the man to the phone during the shot
Close the aperture so the man and the phone both stay sharp
With both sharp, nothing guides the viewer's eye towards the phone.
Zoom in quickly towards the phone as it starts to ring
A fast zoom feels rough and leaves the phone soft if focus is still on the man.
I04.why: This is a rack focus. Moving focus from one subject to another tells the viewer exactly where to look.
I04.video: Depth of Field Explained: Guide to Camera Focus

I04.q: You film a café on your phone, walking from a dark corner to a sunny window. The picture gets brighter and changes colour as you move. How do you fix it for the next take?
options: Tap and hold to fix exposure, and set white balance in pro mode
Turn up the phone's screen brightness before you start
Screen brightness only changes your view, not the recorded video.
Walk more slowly so the phone adjusts more gently
The phone will still change brightness and colour, just more slowly.
I04.why: When exposure and white balance stay fixed, the phone stops adjusting as the scene changes, so the shot looks even.

I04.q: You and a friend film a family function on two cameras. In the edit, the shots must cut together smoothly. What do you agree on before starting?
options: The same frame rate, shutter and white balance on both
Both cameras on auto so each one adjusts to the light
Each camera will make different choices, so colour and brightness will not match.
The same resolution, with the other settings left free
Matching resolution alone leaves motion and colour different between the cameras.
I04.why: Matching motion and colour settings by hand on both cameras makes the shots look like one sequence when you cut between them.

I05.q: At a birthday party, you have one camera and the cake is about to be cut. What do you plan to film?
options: The cut in a wide shot, then the grandmother's face and the child's smile
The cut in one long close-up so you never miss the knife moving
You only get the cake, so the edit has nothing to show how people felt about it.
The cut from three angles: wide, medium and close-up on the knife
These all show the same event, and none of them shows how the family responded.
I05.why: The cake cut tells us what happened. The faces of the people watching tell us why the moment meant something, and give you shots to cut between.

I05.q: You have one hour to film a short scene. What does the shot listing video suggest you do first?
options: Write a short list of shots and rank them from most to least important
Shoot every angle you can think of so the editor has lots of choice
Shooting without a plan wastes time, and you may run out before the key shots.
Write a long, detailed list and try to get through every single shot
A long list with no order means you may miss the shots the scene truly needs.
I05.why: A limited, ranked list makes sure the shots the story depends on get filmed first, even if time runs out.
I05.video: A Director's Guide to Shot Listing

I05.q: You are editing an interview with a sweet shop owner. You remove a long pause from the middle of her answer and her face jumps. What do you do?
options: Lay a shot of her hands packing laddoos over the join while she keeps talking
Add a quick white flash between the two clips so the jump feels planned
A flash draws attention to the edit instead of hiding it.
Leave the jump in, since viewers know interviews are always edited
A visible jump in the face looks careless in this kind of interview.
I05.why: Covering the join with a related detail shot hides the cut, and her voice carries on so the answer still flows.

I05.q: You finish an interview with a tailor and have 20 minutes left in his shop. What should you film?
options: Close shots of his hands, scissors, sewing machine and the cloth he talked about
More angles of his face while he chats, to give you extra choices later
More talking shots will not help you hide cuts in his talking.
Wide shots of the busy street outside to show where the shop is
One wide street shot is useful, but it does not show the details of his work.
I05.why: Details of his work and the things he mentions give you shots to cover edits and to show what he is describing.

I05.q: You film a baraat (wedding procession) moving left to right across your frame. For the next shot, you want a new angle. What do you do?
options: Stay on the same side of the road and shoot from further along the route
Cross to the other side of the road to get the shops in the background
From the other side the procession will move right to left and seem to turn back.
Move to any side you like, since the music will keep the edit connected
Sound does not fix confusing direction, and viewers will still feel lost.
I05.why: Staying on one side keeps the procession moving the same way on screen, so viewers feel it is still heading to the same place.

I05.q: The 180 degree rule video talks about crossing the line. When does crossing it work?
options: When you do it on purpose and let the audience see the camera move across
When the shots are short enough that viewers will not notice the flip
Short shots do not hide a flip, and viewers still feel the change in direction.
When the scene is fast, since quick action hides the change of side
Fast action does not stop the flip from confusing people about where things are.
I05.why: A deliberate crossing, like a camera move across the line that viewers can see, keeps them oriented while changing the feel of the scene.
I05.video: The 180 Degree Rule in Film (and How to Break the Line)

I05.q: You film two shopkeepers talking, one at a time with one camera. In the first shot, the man looks towards the right side of the frame. How do you film the woman?
options: Have her look towards the left side of the frame, just beside the lens
Have her look towards the right side too, so the two shots match
If both look right, they will seem to be looking away from each other.
Have her look straight into the lens for a strong, direct feeling
Looking into the lens makes her talk to the viewer, not to the man.
I05.why: Opposite sides of the frame make the two people seem to face each other when you cut between them.

I05.q: A father stands and talks to his young son, who sits on the floor. You film each in a separate close-up. Where should each one look?
options: The son looks up past the lens and the father looks down past it
Both look straight ahead at lens height so the close-ups look even
Level looks lose the height difference, so they won't seem to see each other.
The son looks down and the father looks up, to make them feel equal
This flips their real positions and confuses the viewer.
I05.why: The angle of the look should match where the other person really is, including height, so the two shots connect.

I05.q: You cut from a wide to a close-up of a dhaba cook flipping a roti, during the flip. The cut still feels jumpy. What do you check first?
options: That the roti is at the same height and spot in both clips at the cut
That both clips are about the same length on the timeline
Clip length does not affect whether the movement lines up at the join.
That the close-up is a little brighter so it stands out from the wide
A brightness change makes the join more visible, not smoother.
I05.why: The cut feels smooth only if the action carries on from the exact same point. If the roti jumps position, the eye catches the join.

I05.q: You film a woman opening a shop shutter, first wide, then close. What do you ask her to do so the edit works?
options: Do the whole action the same way in both shots, from start to end
In the close shot, just do the last part where the shutter goes up
Without the full action you have no overlap to pick a cut point.
Try it a little differently each time so you have more variety
If the action changes, the movement will not match across the cut.
I05.why: Repeating the same full action gives you overlap in both shots, so you can cut at the exact same moment of movement.

I05.q: You interview a weaver. She comes to the part about nearly losing her business. How do you use the camera?
options: Slowly push in on her face while she tells that part
Keep a gentle slider move going through the whole interview
Constant movement has no link to the story, so it adds nothing at the key moment.
Pan around the room to show the looms while she talks about it
Moving away from her face loses the feeling at the most emotional point.
I05.why: A slow move closer at that moment draws the viewer into her feeling. The move has a reason, so it lands.

I05.q: In the camera movement guide, what does a tracking shot do for the viewer?
options: It keeps us beside a character as they move, so we share their path
It adds energy, so it suits most scenes that feel a little slow
The guide links movement to story and feeling, not to fixing slow scenes.
It replaces cutaways, so you need fewer shots later in the edit
The guide ties tracking to following a character, not to saving shots.
I05.why: Following a character keeps us with them through space, which gives both information and emotion. A still shot is often better when a move adds nothing.

I06.q: You are filming a bakery owner under a ceiling tube light. Her eyes look like dark holes. What do you change?
options: Switch off the tube and place a soft light off to her left, angled down a little.
Keep the tube on and add a light right next to the camera, at her eye level.
A light from the camera fills the eyes but makes the face flat, with no shape.
Switch off the tube and place your light low, below her chin, pointing up.
Light from below makes a face look strange and spooky, not natural.
I06.why: The overhead tube causes the eye shadows, so it goes off. A soft light from an angle, slightly high, gives the face gentle shape.

I06.q: The Aputure video compares five interview setups. In the Rembrandt setup, what tells you the light is placed right?
options: A small triangle of light on the cheek that is away from the light.
The whole face is evenly bright, with no shadow on either cheek.
Even, shadowless light is a flat look, not Rembrandt.
The person is a dark shape against a bright background.
That describes the silhouette setup, a different look in the video.
I06.why: Rembrandt lighting puts the key high and to one side, so only a small triangle of light reaches the far cheek. That triangle is the quick check.
I06.video: How to Light an Interview — 5 Quick Easy Setups

I06.q: At noon, direct sun comes through a window and makes a hard patch of light on your subject's face. You have no lights. What do you do?
options: Hang a thin white cloth over the window so the sun spreads out before it reaches her.
Lower the ISO and close the aperture so the bright patch is less strong.
This darkens the image, but the hard edges and shadows stay the same.
Move her closer to the window so the patch covers her whole face.
Closer to direct sun means more harsh light, not softer light.
I06.why: A thin white cloth turns the small, hard sun into a large, even source. Exposure settings change brightness, not hardness.

I06.q: You seat a grandfather for a family interview with a bright window right behind him. His face is too dark. What is the best fix?
options: Turn his chair so the window lights his face from an angle, and shoot from the room side.
Keep the window behind him and raise exposure until his face looks right.
The window will blow out to pure white before his face looks good.
Keep the window behind him and close the curtain on it fully.
Closing it fully removes your only good light and leaves him dull.
I06.why: Window light works best when it falls on the face, not behind it. Turning the subject uses the free light instead of fighting it.

I06.q: You light a shop owner with one LED from the left. The right side of his face is almost black. You have no second light. What do you add?
options: A white foam board on his right side, angled to send some light back onto his face.
A black cloth on his right side, close to his face, to keep it clean.
Black cloth takes light away, so the dark side gets even darker.
Move the LED closer and make it brighter so more light spills around.
A brighter key also brightens the lit side, so the dark side still looks dark next to it.
I06.why: A white surface catches the main light and bounces it into the shadows. It fills the dark side without a second lamp.

I06.q: In a client's home, you bounce your light off a nearby wall to make it gentle. The wall is painted bright yellow. What should you watch for?
options: The face will pick up a yellow tint, so bounce off a white card instead.
The light will become harder, so move the lamp further from the wall.
Bouncing off a wall makes light softer, not harder. Colour is the real issue.
Nothing changes, because bounced light always keeps its original colour.
Bounced light takes on the colour of the surface it hits.
I06.why: Bounced light carries the colour of the surface. A white or neutral surface keeps skin tones natural.

I06.q: You interview a tailor in his shop. A sunny doorway behind him is much brighter than his face, and viewers' eyes keep going there. What do you do first?
options: Partly close the door or hang a dark cloth so the background drops in brightness.
Brighten the whole shot in the edit so his face matches the doorway.
Lifting everything also lifts the doorway, which then turns pure white.
Add a light on the wall around the doorway so the scene looks even.
More light on the background makes it pull attention even more.
I06.why: The eye goes to the brightest part of the frame. Reducing the background light is quicker and cleaner than trying to outshine it.

I06.q: The Aputure video shows a way to shape the shadow side of a face. Why would you put black cloth or a black flag close to that side?
options: It soaks up stray light from walls, so the shadow side stays deeper.
It bounces extra light into the shadow side, so the face looks even.
Black material absorbs light. A white reflector is what bounces light in.
It hides the light stand, so the key can sit right in front of the face.
A key placed straight in front flattens the face and removes the shadow side.
I06.why: Black material absorbs light bouncing off walls and ceilings. This is called negative fill, and it gives the face more shape and mood.
I06.video: The One Dramatic Lighting Technique You Need to Know

I06.q: A table lamp in the corner of your interview frame shows as a glowing white blob. Your subject's exposure is correct. What do you do?
options: Put in a weaker bulb or a dimmer until the lampshade shows detail again.
Raise exposure so the lamp and the face both look bright and lively.
That makes the lamp even more blown out and overexposes the face.
Lower exposure until the lamp shows detail, then brighten the face in the edit.
The face is now too dark, and lifting it later adds noise and looks muddy.
I06.why: A lamp in the shot should glow, not burn out. Dimming the lamp itself keeps detail in the shade and lets the face stay correctly exposed.

I06.q: During a home interview, a floor lamp sits directly behind your subject, so it looks like it grows from her head. What is the best fix?
options: Move the lamp or the camera so the lamp sits off to one side in the frame.
Turn the lamp brighter so it reads as a halo behind her head.
A bright lamp behind the head is even more distracting.
Blur the background more and leave the lamp where it is now.
A blurred lamp still sits behind her head and still distracts.
I06.why: Objects lined up behind a head look odd. A small change in position keeps the lamp adding mood without fighting the face.

I06.q: At an evening sangeet, a man in a dark kurta stands against a dark wall. On the monitor he melts into the background. What helps most?
options: Place a small light behind him, out of frame, aimed at the back of his head.
Add a stronger light straight from the camera position onto him.
Front light flattens his face and does not create an edge.
Raise exposure in the edit until he finally stands out.
This lifts the wall too, so he still blends in.
I06.why: Light from behind draws a bright edge around the person. That edge stands out against a dark background.

I06.q: In Aputure's commercial interview lighting video, why does the team place the subject well away from the background?
options: So the background can be lit on its own and the shot gains depth.
So the key light can be placed behind the camera for even light.
The video moves the subject to control the background, not to flatten the key.
So the room looks smaller and more private on camera.
Distance from the background makes a room feel deeper, not smaller.
I06.why: Space between subject and background lets you shape each one separately. That control creates depth and keeps the person clearly apart.

I07.q: You are filming a shopkeeper as he walks through a busy street market, talking about his spices. Which mic setup will give the cleanest voice?
options: A clip-on lav mic on his shirt, a hand's width below the chin
The camera's built-in mic, with you walking two steps behind
The camera mic is far from his mouth and will pick up mostly market noise.
A boom mic held high above the crowd, out of shot
A boom is hard to keep pointed at a moving speaker in a crowded lane.
I07.why: A lav moves with the speaker and stays near the mouth, so his voice stays strong over the market noise even while he walks.

I07.q: The StudioBinder video on recording sound looks at mic position, room noise and monitoring. When does it say these problems are best solved?
options: On set, while you record, because they are hard to fix later
In the edit, using noise reduction and EQ tools
Editing tools can help a little, but they cannot fully repair a poorly placed mic or a noisy room.
After a test screening, once you know what bothers viewers
By then the shoot is over, and the only fix is an expensive reshoot.
I07.why: The video stresses fixing sound at the source on location. Good placement and careful listening on set save hours of repair work later.
I07.video: Recording Sound for Film — How to Get Pristine Audio

I07.q: At a wedding reception, the bride's uncle starts his speech. Your recorder's meter keeps hitting the red near 0. What do you do?
options: Lower the input gain so his loudest words peak near −12
Leave it, and turn the clip down later in the edit
Sound that hits 0 is clipped (cut off and distorted), and lowering it later does not remove the distortion.
Ask him to step back from the mic while he talks
This disturbs the event and makes the sound thinner and more echoey.
I07.why: Gain is the input volume. Peaks around −15 to −9 leave room for loud moments without distortion, while staying well above background hiss.

I07.q: Halfway through an office interview, you notice a low hum that was not there at the start. The meter levels still look normal. What do you do?
options: Pause politely, find the source, like an AC that switched on, and fix it
Keep going, since the meter shows the levels are still in a good range
Meters show loudness, not quality, so a hum can sit under good levels and ruin the take.
Raise the gain a little so the voice stays clearly above the hum
Higher gain lifts the hum by the same amount, so it stays just as noticeable.
I07.why: Hums and buzzes are only caught by listening. Stopping to remove the cause is far easier than trying to clean it out in the edit.

I07.q: You clip a lav on the bride's mother's silk saree pallu. In your test, you hear rustling each time she moves her arm. What do you do?
options: Move the mic off the loose fabric, tape it, and test again
Turn the gain down so the rustle becomes quieter
This lowers her voice by the same amount, so the rustle stays just as noticeable.
Ask her to keep her arms still during the talk
People forget within minutes, and a stiff posture looks unnatural on camera.
I07.why: Rustle comes from cloth or cable moving against the mic. Securing it in a calmer spot and testing with real movement fixes the cause.

I07.q: In Deity's video on hiding a lav mic, what is the main sound problem the careful hiding method protects against?
options: Cloth and cable rubbing on the mic, which creates scratchy noise
The mic being too far from the mouth to hear speech
Distance matters, but the hiding steps focus on stopping the mic from moving against fabric.
Radio signal drop-outs between the transmitter and receiver
That is a wireless range issue, not what the concealment method is solving.
I07.why: A hidden lav sits under clothing, so it must be fixed in place. Taping and looping the cable stops fabric from rubbing the mic during movement.
I07.video: How To Hide A Lav Microphone

I07.q: A client wants an interview on a Mumbai rooftop. It is windy, and your test recording has loud rumbling. What do you do?
options: Fit a furry windshield and move to a corner sheltered by a wall
Raise the gain so the voice rises above the rumble
Higher gain makes the wind rumble louder too and may cause distortion.
Record anyway and remove the wind with noise reduction
Wind rumble is loud and uneven, and cleaning it often leaves the voice sounding damaged.
I07.why: Wind noise is air hitting the mic itself. A fluffy cover and a sheltered spot stop the air before it reaches the mic, which no edit can fully do.

I07.q: You must interview a fruit vendor next to a busy road. In your test, the traffic roar almost covers his voice. What is the best fix?
options: Clip a lav near his mouth and move to a quieter side lane
Use the camera mic and add noise reduction later
The camera mic is far away, and heavy noise reduction makes the voice sound watery.
Turn up the gain so his voice beats the traffic
Gain raises the traffic as much as the voice, so the balance does not improve.
I07.why: A closer mic makes the voice much louder than the background, and a quieter spot lowers the noise itself. Both help before anything is recorded.

I07.q: You finish an interview in a tailor's shop with a sewing machine humming next door. Before packing up, what should you record?
options: About 30 seconds of the shop in silence, with the same mic in place
A short clip of the sewing machine on its own, up close
That gives a separate sound, not the background that sits behind the speech.
A few quiet wide shots of the shop for the editor to use
Shots help the picture edit, but the editor still has no matching background sound for audio gaps.
I07.why: The editor needs the exact background of that space, recorded with the same setup, to fill gaps and smooth cuts.

I07.q: Your editor cuts out the 'umm's from an interview. Now the background hiss keeps dropping out between words. What helps most?
options: Lay the silent location recording from the shoot under those gaps
Add soft background music to cover the jumps
Music can hide some problems, but it changes the mood and is not right for every film.
Lower the whole interview volume so the gaps are less clear
The hiss still drops in and out, just more quietly, and the voice gets weaker.
I07.why: The quiet recording made on location has the same hiss as the interview, so placing it in the gaps makes the background sound continuous.

I07.q: You are interviewing an elderly sweet-shop owner for a local brand film. He looks stiff, and five family members are watching. What do you do first?
options: Ask most of them to step out, then chat about his shop
Start recording right away so he does not get more nervous
Rushing in keeps him tense, and the first answers usually sound stiff and short.
Hand him the exact questions so he can memorise answers
Memorised answers sound rehearsed and lose the natural feeling you want.
I07.why: An audience adds pressure, and an easy talk first builds trust. He will then answer the camera questions more naturally.

I07.q: Your interviewee answers, 'Yes, it was a good year.' Based on Videomaker's advice on documentary questions, what should you do next?
options: Ask something like 'What made it a good year?' and listen for more
Move on to the next question on your list to save time
You lose the story behind the short answer, which is often the best part.
Ask 'Was it your best year ever?' to get a stronger answer
This is another yes-or-no question and will likely get another short reply.
I07.why: Open questions invite the person to explain. Listening closely and following up turns short replies into complete, usable answers.
I07.video: How to Ask Great Documentary Interview Questions

I07.q: You are filming a factory worker's story about unsafe conditions. Following the WITNESS video on consent, what should you do before recording?
options: Explain where it will be shown and the risks, then get clear agreement
Record first, then ask permission once you see what they said
Consent should come before recording, so the person decides with full knowledge.
Assume agreement because they already agreed to meet you
Agreeing to meet is not the same as understanding and agreeing to how the footage is used.
I07.why: Informed consent means the person knows how the footage will be used and what risks it may bring. They agree freely before you start recording.

I08.q: Your sound recordist hands you a file called room_tone.wav from the shoot. Your project has Footage, Audio and Project folders. Where does it go?
options: In the Audio folder, with the other sound recordings.
In the Footage folder, since it was recorded on the shoot.
Footage is for camera clips, so a sound file there is hard for others to find.
In the Project folder, next to the edit file that uses it.
The Project folder holds edit files, not media, so sound gets lost there.
I08.why: Room tone is a quiet recording of the room's sound, so it is audio. Putting each type of file in the same place every time means anyone can find it.

I08.q: You moved your footage to a new drive. Now Premiere shows your clips as offline. What does the setup video show you should do?
options: Use the link media option to point Premiere to the files' new place.
Import all the clips again and rebuild the edit from scratch.
Rebuilding wastes hours, and the files only need to be reconnected.
Delete the offline clips from the timeline and carry on.
This throws away your edit work when the media can be found and relinked.
I08.why: Relinking tells the project where the files now live, so all your cuts come back as they were.

I08.q: Your 4K camera footage stutters on your laptop timeline. What does the proxy video suggest?
options: Make small proxy copies to edit with, then use the originals for export.
Convert the originals to low quality and delete the big files.
You lose your full quality footage for good, which you need for the final export.
Edit as it is and just export the film at a lower resolution.
A lower export does not fix the stutter while you edit.
I08.why: A proxy is a lighter copy of a clip that plays smoothly while editing. Premiere switches back to the full files when you export.

I08.q: You copied a wedding card to your laptop and the copy finished with no error. What do you do before formatting the card?
options: Compare file count and total size with the card, then play a few clips.
Format the card right away, since the copy showed no error.
Copies can fail silently, so no error message does not prove the files are whole.
Look for thumbnails in the folder, then format the card.
A thumbnail can show even when the rest of the file is broken or cut short.
I08.why: Matching the count and size shows nothing is missing, and playing clips shows the files actually work.

I08.q: You shoot a two-day event and keep a main copy and a backup drive. When is it safe to format the camera cards?
options: Only after each drive matches the card and its clips play.
As soon as the first copy has finished on the laptop.
One unchecked copy is a single point of failure if that drive or file is bad.
Before the next day's shoot, whatever the copies show.
Needing an empty card is not a reason to risk losing a whole day of footage.
I08.why: The card is your original. Keep it until you know every copy is complete and plays.

I08.q: You filmed a sweet shop owner on two different days. Months later the client asks for the second take from 11 March. Which clip name finds it fastest?
options: 2025-03-11_SweetShop_OwnerInt_T02
SweetShop_OwnerInt_T02
There is no date, so you cannot tell which day's take two this is.
2025-03-11_SweetShop_good_final
Words like good and final do not tell you which take it was.
I08.why: This name holds the day, the project, the shot and the take, so a search finds it at once.

I08.q: Why do editors write dates in names as 2025-03-11 and not 11-03-2025?
options: Year first makes files sort in true date order in any folder.
It is the only date format that cameras will accept.
Cameras do not care how you rename files on your computer.
It makes the file name shorter and easier to type.
Both formats have the same number of characters.
I08.why: Computers sort names letter by letter, so year, then month, then day puts clips in the right order.

I08.q: For a saree shop film you shot an owner interview, the shop front and weaving close-ups, out of order over two days. How do you set up your bins?
options: One bin for each scene, like interview, shop front and weaving.
One bin for each shoot day, in the order you filmed.
Each scene is split across both days, so you must search two bins every time.
One bin for each camera card, as the files came off.
Card order says nothing about content, so finding a shot stays slow.
I08.why: Bins by scene put every take of the same moment side by side, so comparing and picking the best one is quick.

I08.q: You have a 50-minute interview. How does the transcription video help you find the usable answers?
options: Read the transcript, highlight the good lines, and add them to the timeline.
Scrub along the audio waveform looking for the loudest parts.
Loud parts are not always good answers, and this is slow for a long interview.
Let the automatic transcript build the final cut on its own.
The transcript helps you find lines, but you still judge and shape the edit.
I08.why: Text-based editing lets you search and pick answers by reading, which is much faster than watching the whole interview.

I08.q: At a sangeet, you recorded speeches on a separate recorder but forgot to clap. The camera also recorded rough sound. How do you sync?
options: Match the camera's rough sound waveform to the recorder's, then watch the mouths.
Line up both files by where each recording begins.
The camera and recorder were almost never started at the same moment.
Play both together and nudge them by ear until it sounds close.
Close by ear is often a few frames off, which viewers notice on faces.
I08.why: The camera sound has the same speech shape as the recorder, so the waveforms line up. Then a visual check confirms it.

I08.q: In the audio mixing video, how does Premiere line up the separate sound recording with the camera clip?
options: It compares the shape of the audio waveforms in both clips.
It needs matching timecode, so both devices must be linked.
The waveform method works even when the devices share no timecode.
It lines clips up by the time each file was created.
File times are rarely exact enough to sync speech.
I08.why: Both devices heard the same sounds, so Premiere can match the peaks and dips of the waveforms.

I08.q: A restaurant client wants new music and a new shot order for their promo. What do you do before you start?
options: Copy the current sequence, label the copy, and edit only the copy.
Change the current sequence and rely on undo if needed.
Undo history is lost when you close the project, so the old cut can vanish.
Export the current cut, then delete the old sequence.
An exported file cannot be edited, so you cannot rework that cut later.
I08.why: The first cut stays untouched, so if the client prefers it, you can return in seconds.

I08.q: After many rounds, the client says they liked the cut you sent last Thursday. Which naming habit lets you find it fast?
options: Promo_v03_2025-06-12, a new number and date each time
Promo_final, then Promo_final_new when it changes
Names like final and new soon pile up and do not show which came when.
Promo, saved over the same file each time
Saving over one file means Thursday's cut no longer exists.
I08.why: A rising number with a date shows the order of every cut, so you can open the right one at once.

I08.q: In the media intelligence video, what do you do with AI search results?
options: Check them against the real footage and pick your selects.
Use every result in the edit.
Search returns near-misses as well as good shots.
Delete the clips the search didn’t find.
Search misses things. Those clips may still be useful.
I08.why: Search narrows things down. You still choose.

I08.q: You search 300 wedding clips for “rings” and get 6. You remember filming more. What next?
options: Skim the ceremony clips to find the ones search missed.
Use the 6 and move on.
You might miss the best ring shot.
Assume the others were deleted.
More likely they just weren’t tagged well.
I08.why: Use search to start, not to finish.

I09.q: You are editing a haldi ceremony video. You have ten minutes of guests arranging chairs and one clip of the bride's grandmother crying as she applies the paste. What do you do?
options: Keep the grandmother clip and trim most of the chair setup.
Keep everything in order so no part of the day is missed.
Long stretches with nothing happening make viewers lose interest fast.
Keep the chair setup because it shows how the day began.
A few seconds can set the scene, but ten minutes of setup carries no feeling.
I09.why: The grandmother's tears carry emotion the family will remember. Setup with no action can shrink to a quick shot or go entirely.

I09.q: In the video, what mainly guides an editor's choice of when and where to cut?
options: The editor's own reaction to the footage, watching it like a viewer.
The tools and shortcuts the editing software offers.
The video talks about the editor's thinking, not the software controls.
A fixed rule about how long each shot should last.
The video shows choices coming from reactions to the footage, not from set lengths.
I09.why: The video explains that editors trust their own response to each moment. If a moment moves you, it will likely move the audience.
I09.video: How Does an Editor Think and Feel?

I09.q: You are making a short film about a woman who runs a small bakery in Pune. How should the film begin?
options: Show early that she wants to open a second shop before Diwali.
Start with a slow tour of every item on her shelves.
Pretty shots alone give viewers no reason to keep watching.
Start with her full life history from childhood.
A long background at the start delays the part people care about.
I09.why: A clear goal near the start gives viewers something to wonder about. They keep watching to find out if she makes it.

I09.q: Halfway through your bakery film, there is a three-minute section about her cousin's shoe shop. It is fun but has nothing to do with her goal. What do you do?
options: Cut it, because it pulls attention away from her goal.
Keep it, because viewers enjoy a break from the main topic.
A long side trip makes viewers forget what they were following.
Move it to the end so it plays after the main story.
Placing it at the end still leaves an unrelated part hanging after the payoff.
I09.why: Every section should move the main thread forward. Side stories, even good ones, make the film harder to follow.

I09.q: You interview a weaver in Varanasi. You join two parts of her answer, and now her face jumps at the edit point. What is the best fix?
options: Place a shot of her hands on the loom over the join.
Add a slow dissolve between the two parts of her answer.
A dissolve on a talking face looks odd and still shows the cut.
Leave the jump, since viewers will not notice it.
A jump in a talking face is easy to see and looks like a mistake.
I09.why: A related shot over the join hides the jump while her voice keeps flowing. It also shows the work she is talking about.

I09.q: You have covered most of the weaver's answer with shots of her work. When is the best time to come back to her face?
options: When she says something emotional, so viewers see her feeling.
Never, so that every edit in her answer stays hidden.
Viewers need to see her sometimes to connect with her as a person.
Every ten seconds, at a fixed and steady rhythm.
A fixed timer ignores what she is saying and may miss her best moments.
I09.why: Her face carries the feeling behind her words. Save it for the moments where her expression adds something the pictures cannot.

I09.q: Your Ganesh festival promo uses one-second shots for two full minutes. Your friend says it feels tiring. What do you change?
options: Hold a few key shots longer, like the idol arriving.
Make every shot even shorter to add more energy.
More of the same speed makes the tiredness worse, not better.
Make every shot three seconds long for a calm feel.
One even speed all through is still flat, just slower.
I09.why: Changing speed gives viewers a moment to breathe. The fast parts then feel more exciting by contrast.

I09.q: According to the video, what should decide the pace of a section?
options: The purpose of the scene and what the viewer should feel there.
A standard shot length that suits most types of video.
The video shows pace changing with the scene, not following one set length.
Cutting as quickly as possible to keep attention high.
The video ties pace to purpose, and speed with no reason soon tires viewers.
I09.why: The video links each pacing choice to its purpose. Tempo changes are planned to serve the story, not added at random.
I09.video: Pacing in Film Editing — Techniques Every High-End Editor Must Know

I09.q: You cut from a quiet morning at home to a loud Crawford Market scene. The noise hits suddenly and feels jarring. What do you try?
options: Start the market noise softly under the last second of the home shot.
Mute the market sound for the first few seconds.
Silence in a busy market feels strange and breaks the mood.
Add a fade to black between the two scenes.
A fade slows things down and still leaves the noise starting abruptly.
I09.why: Letting the new sound begin early prepares the viewer. The change feels smooth and draws them into the next place.

I09.q: At the end of an interview, a shopkeeper says a line you love. You want to cut to shots of him locking up the shop. How do you handle the audio?
options: Let his voice carry on over the first shots of him locking up.
Cut picture and sound at the exact same frame.
A hard cut on both can chop off the feeling of his last line.
Remove his voice and add music over the new shots.
You lose the line you loved, which was the point of the moment.
I09.why: Keeping his voice under the new picture links his words to his actions. This is called an L-cut, where sound from one shot runs into the next.

I09.q: You show a sari shop owner your two-minute promo. At around 0:40, she starts checking her phone. What is the most useful thing to do?
options: Note the time and look closely at what is dragging at that point.
Pause and explain that a better part is coming soon.
Viewers online will not have you there to explain, so the problem stays.
Ignore it and just ask her at the end if she liked it.
People often say they liked it to be polite, so you lose the real signal.
I09.why: Where attention drops is honest feedback. Finding that exact spot tells you what to trim or tighten.

I09.q: What does the video show by cutting the same scene in two different ways?
options: Changing the order and timing of the same shots changes the mood.
A weak scene usually needs new footage to be fixed.
The video uses the same material both times, so reshooting was not needed.
There is one correct cut that skilled editors always find.
Both edits work. They simply create different structures and tones.
I09.why: The same footage can feel tense or calm depending on the edit. So when feedback says a part feels wrong, you can often fix it by re-cutting.
I09.video: How Editors Cut the Same Scene in 2 Completely Different Ways

I09.q: In the Smart Switch video, what do you refine after the AI switches angles?
options: Reactions, how long each shot holds and the timing of the cuts.
Nothing. The AI cut is final.
The AI follows who’s talking, not what matters.
Only the colour of each angle.
Colour helps, but the switches still need editing.
I09.why: The AI makes a first pass. The editor makes it work.

I09.q: In a podcast edit, the AI cuts to the speaker every time. The host laughs at a joke off-camera. What do you do?
options: Cut to the host’s laugh. Reactions bring the moment to life.
Leave it on the speaker.
You lose a reaction that makes the moment fun.
Cut to the wide shot.
The laugh is clearer on the host’s angle.
I09.why: Edit for reactions and story, not just for who’s talking.

I10.q: You interview a shop owner in Chandni Chowk. Back home you hear a steady air-con hum, and her voice sounds boomy because she stood near a wall. What do you do?
options: Use gentle noise reduction for the hum, then cut a little bass with EQ.
Push noise reduction very hard until the hum is completely gone.
Heavy noise reduction makes a voice sound watery and robotic, which is worse than a faint hum.
Add background music loud enough to cover the hum and boom.
Music does not fix the voice, and it makes her words harder to hear.
I10.why: Noise reduction handles steady sounds like hum. EQ (changing the balance of low and high tones) fixes boom. A light touch with each keeps the voice natural.

I10.q: In the Adobe video, a tool lowers the music automatically whenever someone starts speaking. What is this called?
options: Ducking
Normalising
Normalising sets a whole clip to one target loudness. It does not react to speech.
Noise gating
A noise gate cuts quiet sounds on a track. It does not lower music under a voice.
I10.why: Ducking dips the music under speech and brings it back up in the gaps, so the voice always stays clear.

I10.q: You join two takes of a speaker at a seminar. Right at the join you hear a small click. What do you do?
options: Blend the two audio clips together over just a few frames.
Blend the two clips over two full seconds so it is smooth.
A long overlap makes both takes play at once, and the words turn into mush.
Lower the volume of both clips around the join.
The click is still there, and now the voice also dips in volume.
I10.why: A crossfade of a few frames removes the sudden jump in the sound wave that causes the click, without anyone noticing the blend.

I10.q: You are removing an "umm" from the middle of a sentence in an interview. Where should you place your cuts on the waveform (the drawing of the sound on your timeline)?
options: In the short pauses where the waveform is almost flat.
In the middle of a word, where the waveform is tall.
Cutting through loud sound creates pops and chopped words.
Wherever the picture looks best, ignoring the waveform.
A good picture cut can still leave a harsh jump in the audio.
I10.why: Near-silent spots give the cleanest joins. Cutting through loud sound is the most common cause of clicks.

I10.q: You finish filming interviews in a hall at a family wedding. Before you pack up, what extra recording will help most in the edit?
options: About 30 seconds of the empty room with everyone staying quiet.
Some extra close-up shots of the decorations and flowers.
Useful footage, but it does nothing to smooth the sound between cuts.
A quick mic test with each guest saying their name.
This checks the mic, but gives you nothing to fill gaps in the edit.
I10.why: This recording, called room tone, is the quiet sound of the space. Laid under the edit, it fills the gaps when you trim pauses.

I10.q: You edit a street market interview. Each time you trim a pause, the crowd noise jumps in and out. How do you fix it?
options: Run a clean stretch of crowd noise from the market under every shot.
Remove all the crowd noise with strong noise reduction.
The voice ends up sounding strange and empty, as if the market vanished.
Add a quick fade out and fade in at every single cut.
The noise now dips at each cut, which still draws attention to the edits.
I10.why: A continuous layer of crowd sound hides the jumps, so the cuts feel smooth and the place feels real.

I10.q: An NGO hires you for a short film about a farmer struggling after a drought. The client sends an upbeat dance track to use. What do you do?
options: Suggest a slower, gentler track and explain why it suits the story.
Use the dance track as it is, since the client picked it.
The cheerful music will clash with the story and confuse viewers.
Use the dance track but keep it very low in the mix.
Even quietly, the bright rhythm still pulls against the serious mood.
I10.why: Music tells viewers how to feel. Part of your job is to guide clients toward music that supports their message.

I10.q: In Curtis Judd's demonstration, how does the music behave while someone is speaking?
options: It stays clearly quieter than the voice but never fully disappears.
It plays at about the same level as the voice to add energy.
Music at voice level competes with the words, and viewers miss what is said.
It is switched off completely every time anyone says a word.
Cutting music off and on constantly sounds choppy and draws attention.
I10.why: The music stays present but clearly underneath, so it supports the scene without covering the dialogue.
I10.video: Mix music behind dialogue — Sound for Video Session

I10.q: You make a phone reel at a dosa stall. The sizzle when batter hits the hot tawa was not captured well. What do you do?
options: Add a clean sizzle sound, timed to the moment the batter lands.
Add a dramatic whoosh sound as the batter is poured.
A whoosh does not match what we see, so the moment feels fake.
Leave that part silent and let the music carry it.
Without the sizzle, the food loses the sound that makes it feel real.
I10.why: A real sound that matches the action, in perfect sync, makes the image feel solid and appetising.

I10.q: You add a door-closing sound to a scene in a small office. It sounds fake. What is the most likely reason?
options: It is louder than the scene and has none of the room's echo.
It needs more bass so it feels heavier and more real.
Extra bass usually makes a mismatched sound stand out even more.
It should be spread wide across left and right speakers.
Wide spreading does not fix a sound that does not match the room.
I10.why: Effects must match the level and echo of the place on screen. Lower it and add a little room sound so it blends.

I10.q: dB (decibels) measures loudness. In a wedding film, the father's speech peaks around -12 dB and the music around -14 dB. What do you change?
options: Bring the music down to around -24 dB under the speech.
Raise the speech to 0 dB so it sits above the music.
0 dB is the very top limit, so the voice will distort and clip.
Leave both, since viewers can turn up the volume.
Turning up raises the music too, so the words stay hard to hear.
I10.why: The speech should lead, with music roughly 10 dB or more below it, so every word comes through.

I10.q: In the Adobe workshop with John Knowles, why are dialogue, music and effects kept on separate tracks?
options: So each type of sound can be set and adjusted on its own.
So the final video file exports faster from the editor.
Track layout is about control of the mix, not export speed.
So one volume setting can be applied to every sound.
It is the opposite: each layer needs its own level and treatment.
I10.why: Separate tracks let you shape the speech first, then place music and effects underneath it on purpose.

I10.q: Your mix for a small business ad sounds perfect on good headphones. What should you do before delivering it?
options: Play it on a phone speaker and cheap earphones to check it.
Boost the whole mix a little so it sounds stronger.
Making everything louder does not tell you if the balance works for viewers.
Deliver it, since good headphones show the true sound.
Most people watch on phones, where music can easily bury the speech.
I10.why: Checking on the devices your audience uses shows whether the speech stays clear above the music.

I10.q: In the RX 11 video, what do you compare before putting the repaired dialogue back?
options: Clarity, artefacts and how much natural room sound is left.
Only the loudness.
Loudness is one part. Artefacts and room sound matter too.
Nothing. Repaired audio is always better.
Over-processing can sound worse than the original.
I10.why: Fix, compare and keep it natural.
I10.video: Remove Background Noise with RX 11 + Audio Post-production Tips

I10.q: You remove all the echo from a voice recorded in a big hall. Now it sounds like a different room from the pictures. What do you do?
options: Leave a little room sound so it matches what viewers see.
Remove the echo from every clip.
The sound should still feel like the place on screen.
Add music over it.
That hides the problem without fixing it.
I10.why: Sound should match the space on screen.

I11.q: You made a warm look on a mehendi clip shot by a window. You paste it onto a clip shot under yellow bulbs, and that clip turns far too orange. What do you do?
options: Correct the second clip's white balance and brightness first, then paste the same look.
Lower the strength of the look on the second clip until it seems right.
The base difference is still there, and the two clips no longer share one style.
Build a separate new look for the second clip from scratch.
This takes more time, and the two clips will not share one style.
I11.why: One look gives the same result only when clips start from a similar, neutral base. Correct each clip on its own, then the shared look works on both.

I11.q: You put a LUT (a preset file that gives a colour look) on a shop promo clip that was shot too dark. Now it looks muddy. What is the best fix?
options: Take the LUT off, correct the clip underneath, then put the LUT back on.
Try a stronger LUT so the new look covers the muddy areas.
A stronger look on a dark clip only makes the mud worse.
Keep the LUT and add sharpening so the clip looks cleaner.
Sharpening does not fix brightness and can add noise to dark areas.
I11.why: A LUT expects a normal starting image. If the clip is wrong underneath, correct that first and the LUT will look as intended.

I11.q: You are editing on a laptop in a sunny room. A face looks fine to you, but the waveform shows it sitting very low. What do you do?
options: Go by the waveform and lift the face, since the bright room changes how the screen looks.
