Leave it as it is, because it looks fine on your screen right now.
Room light and screen settings change what you see, so the clip may look dark elsewhere.
Turn your laptop brightness up until the face looks bright enough.
This changes only your screen, not the video, so viewers will still see it dark.
I11.why: A waveform measures the real brightness of the video. Your view depends on your screen and room, which can mislead you.

I11.q: In the Adobe correction and grading demonstration, what are the colour controls used for across the sequence?
options: To correct each shot and make the shots look consistent with each other.
To give each shot its own different creative look for variety.
Different looks on each shot would make the sequence feel broken, not consistent.
To push saturation up so all the footage looks more lively.
The demonstration is about correcting and matching, not simply adding more colour.
I11.why: The video shows correction and matching as the main job of the colour tools, so the sequence plays as one smooth piece.

I11.q: You filmed a shopkeeper interview with two cameras. Camera B looks bluer and slightly darker than camera A. What do you do?
options: Adjust camera B to match camera A, comparing frames of the same face.
Leave it, since viewers accept that each angle looks a bit different.
Viewers notice when cutting between angles makes the colour jump.
Make both cameras much warmer so the blue difference is hidden.
Warming both keeps the gap between them and adds a new problem.
I11.why: When you cut between angles, both should feel like the same room and moment. Comparing the same face gives a clear reference.

I11.q: In the Adobe video, what does the Color Match tool do?
options: It compares a shot with a reference shot and adjusts it to match.
It adds a ready-made film look to every clip at the same time.
That describes a preset or LUT, not a matching tool.
It sets the brightest and darkest points of a single shot.
That is closer to what Curves or levels do on one shot.
I11.why: Color Match uses a neighbouring or reference image as a target, then shifts the colour of your shot towards it.
I11.video: Create a professional look using Color Match and Curves

I11.q: At a family function lit by tube lights, your aunt's face looks slightly greenish. What is the best fix?
options: Move the tint a little towards magenta while watching the faces.
Raise saturation so her face looks more colourful and alive.
More saturation makes the green stronger, not weaker.
Warm the whole shot strongly until the green is gone.
Heavy warming pushes skin towards orange instead of fixing the green.
I11.why: Tint controls the green to magenta balance. A small move towards magenta cancels the green that tube lights often add.

I11.q: You use a vectorscope (a scope that shows which way colours lean and how strong they are) to check skin. What should you look for?
options: Skin sitting near the skin tone guide line, whatever the person's complexion.
Skin pulled to the centre so it shows almost no colour at all.
The centre means grey, so skin there would look lifeless.
Darker skin moved away from the line to make it look fairer.
All healthy skin tones sit near the same line, so this makes skin look unnatural.
I11.why: Skin of every complexion falls close to one guide line on the vectorscope. Only brightness differs, so the line is a reliable check.

I11.q: For a small bakery ad, you add a strong teal look you love. Now the cakes look grey-blue. What do you do?
options: Ease the look back so the cakes keep their real, tasty colours.
Keep it strong, since bold looks make ads feel modern.
If the product looks unappetising, the ad fails no matter how stylish it is.
Use the look on only some shots to add some variety.
Mixing graded and ungraded shots makes the ad look inconsistent.
I11.why: The grade should help sell the cakes. A gentle look keeps the food appealing and keeps attention on the product.

I11.q: Your log footage (a flat recording mode that keeps more detail) looks washed out. Following the Color Management video, what should you do first?
options: Set how the software reads the footage's colour, so it displays correctly.
Add any LUT that looks good and adjust things from there.
A random LUT may not suit your camera's format and can clip colours.
Raise contrast and saturation by hand until it looks right.
Guessing by hand is slow and rarely gets the colours accurate.
I11.why: The video explains that correct input and colour management settings show the footage properly before any creative work.

I12.q: You add a white title over a shot of a bright sky at a wedding venue. On your phone, the words almost vanish. What do you do?
options: Add a soft dark shadow or band behind the words
Make the white letters thinner and more stylish
Thin letters are even harder to see on a bright background.
Leave it, since viewers can pause the video
Most people will not pause, so they will just miss the title.
I12.why: White on a bright sky has almost no contrast. A shadow or dark band separates the words from the background so they stand out.

I12.q: Your end card for a tailor shop shows the address and phone number. It sits near the bottom corner and lasts one second. What do you change?
options: Move it in from the edges and hold it for about four seconds
Keep the spot but use a fancier script font for style
A fancy font is harder to read and does not fix the edge or timing problem.
Keep the timing but make the letters smaller and neater
Smaller text is harder to read, and one second is still too fast.
I12.why: Text near the edge can be cut off or hidden by app buttons. Viewers need a few seconds to read a number, ideally twice.

I12.q: You are editing a family function film. The bride's aunt, Meena Iyer, gives a short speech. Which on-screen title do you use?
options: Meena Iyer, Bride's Aunt
Meena
A first name alone does not tell viewers who she is to the couple.
Meena Iyer, who came from Chennai to bless the couple
This is too long to read before the title disappears.
I12.why: A full name plus one short role tells the viewer everything they need, fast.

I12.q: A client wants their owner's title to read: "Ravi Kumar, Founder, CEO, Master Chef and Award Winner since 2005". What do you suggest?
options: Pick the one role that matters most for this video
Keep every role but shrink the font to make it fit
Tiny text with many words is hard to read in a few seconds.
Keep every role and split it over three lines
Three lines is still too much to read while he is talking.
I12.why: One clear role is easy to read. Extra details can go in the voiceover or description.

I12.q: You watch back your captions on an interview. Each line appears about one second before the person starts saying it. What do you do?
options: Shift each line so it starts when the voice starts
Leave it, since early captions give more reading time
Captions that run ahead confuse viewers and can spoil what comes next.
Make every line longer so the gap is less noticeable
Longer lines are harder to read and the timing is still wrong.
I12.why: Captions should appear with the spoken words. Then viewers can read and listen together.

I12.q: In the captioning video, the speech is turned into text automatically first. What should you do before creating the caption lines?
options: Read the transcript and fix names and wrong words
Pick the caption font and colour straight away
Styling comes later. Mistakes in the text matter more.
Trust the transcript and move on to the timing
Automatic transcripts often get names and local words wrong.
I12.why: The workflow goes from transcription to captions to styling. Fixing the text early means every caption is correct.
I12.video: Improve video accessibility using captioning tools

I12.q: You turn a wide shop promo into a vertical Reel. In one shot, the price board on the left is now cut off. What do you do?
options: Move the crop on that shot so the board shows
Leave it, since most of the shots look fine
One cut-off price can lose the whole message of the ad.
Go back and shrink the whole video with black bars
Black bars waste the vertical screen and make everything small.
I12.why: A new shape can hide different things in each shot. Fix the shots that need it, one by one.

I12.q: In the reframe video, the automatic crop does not follow the subject well in one part. How is it fixed?
options: Add position and scale keyframes to adjust the crop
Run the automatic tool again until it gets it right
Running it again usually gives the same result.
Delete that part of the clip from the vertical version
Cutting the clip loses content when a simple adjustment would work.
I12.why: Keyframes are markers that set the frame's position and size at a moment. They let you guide the crop by hand where the tool misses.
I12.video: Reframe your video for multiple social platforms

I12.q: A sweet shop wants a 15-second cut of their 60-second ad. What do you build it from?
options: A strong opening, the best making shot and the shop name
The first 15 seconds of the ad, exactly as it is
You lose the shop name and the best moment at the end.
A fast montage of as many shots as will fit
Too many quick shots and no clear ending leave viewers confused.
I12.why: A short cut still needs a start that grabs, the moment that sells and a clear finish.

I12.q: You are cutting a 3-minute wedding film down to 1 minute. Which parts do you remove first?
options: Middle shots that repeat what other shots already show
The opening shots, so the film gets going faster
The opening is what makes people keep watching.
The last emotional moment, since it runs the longest
That moment is the payoff the whole film leads to.
I12.why: Repeated shots add time but not story. Cutting them keeps the start, the big moment and the ending.

I12.q: You finished a 16:9 YouTube edit for a gym. They also want it as an Instagram Reel. How do you export the Reel?
options: A reframed vertical file at 1080 by 1920
The same 16:9 file, since Instagram will adjust it
Instagram shows it small with empty space, not filling the phone screen.
A 4K 16:9 file, so the quality stays high
Higher resolution does not fix the wrong shape for a vertical Reel.
I12.why: Reels use a 9:16 vertical shape. Exporting at that size fills the phone screen.

I12.q: In the Frame.io review video, how does a reviewer point to an exact problem in your edit?
options: They leave a comment tied to that moment's timecode
They send a long email listing all their notes
Email notes are hard to match to the exact frame they mean.
They download the file and mark it up themselves
The video shows comments made right on the uploaded version.
I12.why: Timecoded comments are linked to an exact point in the video. You jump straight there, fix it and upload a new version.
I12.video: Enhance your review process with Frame.io

I13.q: A sweet shop owner in Pune wants a Diwali video. You planned a 3-minute cinematic film. Then he says it will go on WhatsApp status for his regular customers. What do you change?
options: Make it short and vertical, with the offer and shop name shown early.
Keep the 3-minute film and send him a link he can forward.
Status viewers watch on phones for a few seconds, so a long film will not get the offer seen.
Keep the plan but add more slow motion shots of the sweets.
Nicer shots do not fix a video that is the wrong length and shape for where it plays.
I13.why: Where the video plays and what the owner needs from it should shape length, framing and what goes first. A plan made before knowing this often has to change.

I13.q: In the ceremony walkthrough, why does the filmmaker settle on recording positions before the ceremony begins?
options: Moments like the vows happen only once, so you must already be in place.
So the couple can approve each camera angle before the guests arrive.
Couples rarely approve angles; the real reason is that key moments cannot be repeated.
Because staying in fixed spots makes colour grading much easier later.
Positions are about not missing moments, not about saving time in the grade.
I13.why: A ceremony cannot be paused or redone. Planning positions ahead means you capture each unrepeatable moment cleanly.
I13.video: How to Film a Wedding Ceremony

I13.q: In the planning section, how does researching the couple and the day's timing help with establishing shots?
options: You know where and when to film wide venue shots before it gets busy.
You can skip establishing shots when the day's timeline looks tight.
Establishing shots set the scene; good timing lets you fit them in, not drop them.
You can leave all the wide shots until after the event has ended.
After the event the decor, light and mood are gone, so the shots will not match.
I13.why: Knowing the people, place and schedule lets you plan short windows to grab the wide shots that set the scene.
I13.video: Planning, Gear and Establishing Shots — Wedding BTS Part 1

I13.q: You are filming your nephew's school annual day with one camera. His dance lasts three minutes. What do you make sure you get first?
options: A clear, steady shot of him dancing, with clean sound from the stage.
Slow motion shots of parents clapping and cheering in the crowd.
Crowd reactions are nice extras, but the family mainly wants his performance.
A wide shot of the school building and the decorated gate outside.
Useful for context, but it can be filmed any time, unlike his three minutes on stage.
I13.why: The one thing that cannot be redone is his performance. Secure it with good sound before anything else.

I13.q: You arrive late to film a small business owner's interview and have only 20 minutes. What do you shoot?
options: The interview with clean sound, then a few quick shots of the product and shop.
A smooth slider move for the opening, then the interview if time is left.
A fancy opening is useless if the interview, the heart of the video, is rushed or missed.
Creative B-roll first while the light is good, then a quick interview.
B-roll (extra shots to cut over the talk) supports the interview but cannot replace it.
I13.why: Under time pressure, capture the shots the video cannot work without. Extras only come after.

I13.q: You have three hours of footage from your cousin's sangeet and need a 5-minute film. Where do you start the edit?
options: Pick the key moments and arrange them in order to build the main flow.
Colour grade every clip first so all the footage looks consistent.
Grading clips you will later cut out wastes hours; colour comes near the end.
Choose the music and add transitions before placing any clips.
Transitions and polish cannot fix a film whose basic flow is not yet built.
I13.why: A rough cut that shows the main events in a clear order comes first. Pace, sound and colour all depend on it.

I13.q: A boutique client wants a 3-minute YouTube film and a vertical Instagram Reel from the same shoot. When do you make the Reel?
options: After the main edit is approved and its sound and colour are done.
At the very start, so both edits can grow side by side together.
Editing two cuts in parallel means every story change has to be done twice.
Before colour work, since phone screens hide most colour problems.
Phone viewers notice poor colour too, and the Reel should match the main film.
I13.why: Making extra formats from a finished, approved edit saves rework and keeps every version consistent.

I14.q: A sweet shop owner in Pune wants an Instagram video. When you ask who it is for, she says "everyone". What do you do?
options: Ask who buys from her most often, and agree on that group as the main viewer.
Accept it and plan a general video that tries to please every age group.
A video made for everyone usually speaks clearly to no one.
Leave the viewer open for now and decide once you see which footage looks best.
The viewer should shape the shoot, not be picked after it.
I14.why: A clear main viewer guides the tone, music and length. Agreeing on it now saves you from wasted shooting or a reshoot later.

I14.q: In the brief framework from the video, which part protects you from extra work you never priced?
options: The scope, which lists clearly what is included and what is not.
The audience, which describes who will watch the finished video.
Audience shapes the content but does not set limits on the work.
The objectives, which describe what the client wants the video to do.
Objectives explain the purpose, but they do not fence in the amount of work.
I14.why: Scope sets the boundaries of the job. When the client asks for more later, you can point to it and discuss extra time or cost.

I14.q: You scout a client's office in Gurgaon at 10 am. The interview is booked for 4 pm in the same room, next to a big window. What should you do?
options: Go back at 4 pm, or check the sun's path, because the window light will change.
Note the light as it looks now, since the room and the window will not move.
The sun moves, so the light at 4 pm can be very different from 10 am.
Plan to close the curtains fully, so the time of day will not matter at all.
This throws away a useful light source without first knowing if it is a problem.
I14.why: Light changes through the day. You need to see or predict the light at the real shoot time, not the scout time.

I14.q: On a technical scout, why does the video stress checking power sockets and supply?
options: So your lights and chargers will not trip the power or need cables you did not bring.
So you can put the camera right next to a socket and skip carrying batteries.
The point is knowing the load and cable runs, not tying the camera to one spot.
So you can decide which camera lens to use in each part of the location.
Lens choice depends on space and framing, not on where the sockets are.
I14.why: A tripped circuit or a missing extension cord can stop a shoot. Knowing the power setup lets you plan cables, batteries and load in advance.

I14.q: You are filming a haldi ceremony. A cousin and a friend have offered to help you. How do you use them?
options: One watches the mic and audio levels. The other handles batteries, cards and the shot list.
Give both a phone to film extra angles of whatever looks interesting to them.
Untargeted extra footage is hard to edit and leaves sound and gear unwatched.
Tell both to stay close and help with whatever you need at each moment.
Vague help means you keep giving orders and things still get missed.
I14.why: A fixed task for each person means sound and gear are always covered, and you can focus on the camera.

I14.q: Halfway through a shop shoot, you notice your sound helper keeps moving lights, and some audio has clipped (become distorted from being too loud). What do you do?
options: Ask them to return to sound only, and move the lights yourself or with the other helper.
Thank them for helping with lights and fix the audio problems later in the edit.
Clipped audio usually cannot be repaired properly in the edit.
Take over the sound yourself so they can keep helping with the lights.
You now juggle camera and sound, which spreads your own attention too thin.
I14.why: Keeping each person on their own task stops gaps like clipped audio. Calmly reset roles as soon as they drift.

I14.q: You have shot a product video for a small saree business. You want to finish the colour and music fully before the client sees anything. What is the better move?
options: Send a rough cut first to check the story and order before spending time on polish.
Finish everything first so the client sees only your best and most complete work.
If they want story changes, all the polish time on those parts is wasted.
Wait until the client asks to see progress, so you are not disturbing them.
Waiting delays feedback and makes late changes more likely and more costly.
I14.why: A quick check-in at the rough cut stage catches big changes early, when they are cheap to make.

I14.q: A client replies on WhatsApp: "Fix the bit near the end." Using the review workflow in the video, what do you do?
options: Ask them to leave a comment in the review link, pinned to the exact timecode.
Guess which part they mean, change it, and send a fresh file on WhatsApp.
Guessing can change the wrong part and mixes up which version is current.
Call them and write their notes in a notebook while you both play the video.
Notes taken this way are loose and not tied to exact moments or versions.
I14.why: Timecoded comments (notes linked to an exact point in the video) remove guessing, and new versions stay in one place for easy comparison.

I14.q: Your rough cut feels flat, even though every shot is fine on its own. Based on the pacing video, what would you try?
options: Mix quicker stretches with slower moments so the energy rises and falls.
Cut every shot shorter so the whole video moves faster from start to end.
Uniform fast cutting can feel just as flat as uniform slow cutting.
Make all the shots the same length so the video has a steady rhythm.
An even rhythm is exactly what makes a cut feel flat and predictable.
I14.why: Changing pace gives the viewer contrast. Slower moments let things land, and faster parts lift the energy.
